**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions. TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question (1A\* or 1B\*). Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A - CAMEROON SINCE 1850.** Question one is compulsory. Answer either 1A\* or 1B\* and one other Question from this section.

**1A\* (Starred question)**

Study this extract on the First World War in Cameroon and its consequences and answer questions (a) to (e) which follow. (The maximum mark for each sub question is indicated in brackets)

> In the month of ...the Allied powers decided to extend the First World War to Cameroon after taking into consideration a number of reasons...Forces from three European countries launched an attack on German Kamerun which led to the rapid fall of the coastal strategic town of ... in which a provisional administration was proposed to be set up. Although the Germans resisted for long, in February 1916, their resistance was finally crushed ... **[line 5]**
>
> ...Diplomacy relating to the ex-enemy territory after the war concerned two Allied powers that took part in the Cameroon campaign. Their discussions and actions had far reaching consequences on the people of the defeated territory...
>
> Seemingly uninterested in making territorial gains in Cameroon, His Majesty's Government felt obliged to accede to the desires of the French Government that with the exceptions of some portions, the whole of the Cameroons should be administered by the French during the last stages of the war. **[line 10]**
>
> ...The British officer laid out the maps of Cameroon and asked his French counterpart what part of Kamerun the French would like, supposing he were in a position to meet their wishes. It never dawned on him to ask for the whole of the Kamerun. He therefore traced on the map an enormous area about 143000 squares miles or four-fifths of that territory...The French official was happy to be able to agree then and there to this proposal and asked him to inform his government accordingly... **[line 15]**
>
> ...Further diplomatic negotiations between the two powers brought together from the two countries respectively the Minister of Colonies and Foreign Secretary to produce a landmark agreement partitioning the territory. This agreement was approved by an international treaty in 1919 by which the defeated enemy power formally relinquished her hold over Cameroon with devastating economic consequences on Cameroonians. **[line 20]**

*Source: Adapted and edited by Panel.*
incertitudes: Question 1A* : le texte du sujet comporte des blancs (mois et année, villes) et le sujet ne donne pas ses réponses attendues ; les blancs sont comblés par l'historiographie courante : août 1914 pour l'extension de la guerre au Cameroun, Douala pour la ville stratégique (tombée le 27 septembre 1914), Anglo-French Condominium pour l'administration provisoire. Le point de départ exact de la guerre au Cameroun (fin juillet-août 1914) varie selon les ouvrages ; « August 1914 » est la réponse la plus courante.

1A* (c)(i) et (c)(ii) : l'accord anglo-français de partage est daté de mars 1916 ; le nom du fonctionnaire britannique (Sir Charles Strachey, du Colonial Office, face à Georges Picot) est celui que donnent les manuels courants ; il n'a pas pu être confirmé sur une source, et un historien devrait le relire.

1A* (d)(ii) : le sujet demande « Minister of Colonies » et « Foreign Secretary » ; la déclaration Milner-Simon (10 juillet 1919) est signée par Henri Simon (ministre français des Colonies) et Lord Milner (secrétaire d'État britannique aux Colonies, et non Foreign Secretary). Le corrigé accepte les deux noms et signale l'écart de l'intitulé.

Numérotation des lignes : les repères imprimés « 5, 10, 15, 20 » sont placés dans l'énoncé à l'endroit où ils figurent à la marge du sujet ; les renvois « line N » des questions suivent la numérotation du sujet.

1A* (e) : l'énoncé dit que la fin de l'administration allemande a eu « devastating economic consequences » sans les préciser ; le corrigé propose trois conséquences admises par l'historiographie (terres et emplois des plantations, partage et rupture des échanges, charges de guerre) sans chiffre.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Write down the month and year the First World War was extended to Cameroon.
(ii) Name **two** Allied Powers (*line 1*) who decided to extend the First World War to Cameroon.
(iii) Name the strategic coastal town (*line 3*) which fell rapidly to the Allies following the Allied attack on Cameroon.

(2+2+1 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) August 1914 [2 marks: month and year].** The war began in Europe in the summer of 1914. The first Allied attacks on German Kamerun came in August 1914, when British forces from Nigeria and French forces from French Equatorial Africa crossed the frontiers. (The blank in the extract is filled with the usual textbook date.)

**(ii) Britain and France [1 mark each].** The extract speaks of forces from three European countries: Britain, France and, with a smaller contingent, Belgium. The two Allied powers that decided on the campaign and later shared the territory were Britain (Great Britain) and France.

**(iii) Douala [1 mark].** Douala, the main port of Kamerun, with its harbour and wireless station, surrendered to the Allies on 27 September 1914 after a combined naval and land attack.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Give **two** reasons (*line 2*) considered by the Allied powers before extending the First World War to Cameroon.
(ii) What was the name of the proposed provisional administration (*line 3*) set up in the strategic town mentioned in a (iii) above?
(iii) Give any **two** reasons why the Germans were able to resist the Allies (*line 4*) up to 1916.

(2+1+2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Any two reasons [2 marks].**
(1) *Strategic position.* German Kamerun bordered British Nigeria and French Equatorial Africa, so a hostile German colony was a military threat to the Allied territories next to it.
(2) *Douala harbour and wireless station.* The port and the wireless station could serve German warships and German communications with Berlin, so the Allies wanted to destroy them.
(3) *Rejection of neutrality.* The Germans proposed that the colonies should stay neutral under the Berlin Act of 1885, but the Allies refused because they wanted to remove German power from Africa.
(4) *Economic and territorial interests.* Kamerun was rich in plantations (cocoa, bananas, rubber, palm products) and the Allies wished to gain territory and resources.

**(ii) The Anglo-French Condominium [1 mark].** After the fall of Douala in 1914 Britain and France set up a joint (provisional) administration called the Anglo-French Condominium, which lasted until the partition of 1916.

**(iii) Any two reasons [2 marks].**
(1) The Germans had a trained colonial force (the *Schutztruppe*) with African soldiers who knew the land, and they had built forts and defensive positions, for example at Mora and in the interior.
(2) The difficult terrain and climate (dense forest, rivers, the rainy season, tropical diseases) slowed the Allied advance and caused heavy sickness among the attackers.
(3) The Allied forces were separate national columns with poor coordination, long supply lines and little transport.
(4) The Germans withdrew inland to Yaounde and used the interior and the northern strongholds, so the Allies had to fight a long campaign. Their resistance ended in February 1916 (Mora fell that month) and many Germans escaped into Spanish Guinea.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) In which year did His Majesty's Government decide to accede to the desire (*line 10*) of the French Government to have much of Cameroon?
(ii) Who was the British officer who initially held discussions with the French official to accede to the French desires mentioned above in c(i)?
(iii) What proportion of the territory of Cameroon was allowed to France?

(1+1+1 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) 1916 [1 mark].** The Anglo-French agreement dividing the territory in principle dates from March 1916, during the war.

**(ii) Sir Charles Strachey [1 mark].** He was the British Colonial Office official who held the talks with the French official Georges Picot; the arrangement is often called the Strachey-Picot agreement.

**(iii) Four-fifths (4/5, about 80 per cent) [1 mark].** The extract itself says that about 143000 square miles, or four-fifths of the territory, was traced for France. France therefore received the larger part and Britain the remaining one-fifth, which became the British Cameroons.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) In what year did the Trusteeship period begin in French Cameroon?
(ii) Give the name of (a) Minister of Colonies (b) Foreign Secretary, of the two powers that produced the landmark agreement partitioning Cameroon in 1919.
(iii) Which international treaty in 1919 approved the partitioning of Cameroon.

(1+2+1 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) 1946 [1 mark].** The United Nations approved the Trusteeship Agreement for French Cameroon in December 1946, replacing the League of Nations mandate.

**(ii) Henri Simon and Lord Milner [2 marks].** The landmark agreement was the Milner-Simon Declaration of 10 July 1919. Henri Simon was the French Minister of Colonies. The British signatory was Lord Milner, the Secretary of State for the Colonies (the extract and the question loosely call the British representative "Foreign Secretary"). Candidates who give these two names get both marks.

**(iii) The Treaty of Versailles (1919) [1 mark].** By it (Article 119) Germany gave up all her overseas possessions, including Kamerun. The Anglo-French division set out in the Milner-Simon Declaration was then confirmed by League of Nations mandates in 1922.
themes: partition of cameroon after world war one

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) Outline the devastating economic consequences on Cameroonians as a result of the end of German administration (*line 20*).

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Three points [1 mark each].**
1. *Loss of land and jobs on the plantations.* The war and the departure of the Germans disrupted the plantation economy on which many Cameroonians depended for wages. In the British zone the former German plantations were sold by auction in the 1920s, and most of them returned to German owners, so the local people (for example the Bakweri of Mount Cameroon) did not recover the land they had lost to the Germans.
2. *Disruption of trade and division of communities.* The partition between Britain and France cut across ethnic groups, families and old trade routes, and the Duala middlemen and other traders lost markets and contacts in the interior.
3. *War damage and heavy burdens.* The fighting destroyed farms, villages and infrastructure and caused food shortages; the new administrations demanded taxes, porters and labour, so the economic life of ordinary Cameroonians was weakened in the early years after the war.
themes: partition of cameroon after world war one
